name: Growth, Mastery, and Proficiency
title: Growth, Mastery, and Proficiency
answer: Growth data shows how much students have learned over time, while proficiency data shows where they stand against a standard, and both matter because a school with students far behind may show strong growth while proficiency stays low. Reports should show both so progress is not hidden and gaps are not ignored. Standards mastery dashboards and cohort trend analysis extend this by showing which standards each student has mastered and whether groups of students are doing better over the years.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: This idea is about using three connected views of student learning rather than a single number. Growth data captures how much a student has learned over time, while proficiency data captures where that student stands against a standard. A school whose students start far behind may show strong growth even while proficiency remains low, so looking at only one measure can mislead. Reports should show both, so progress is not hidden and gaps are not ignored. Standards mastery dashboards and cohort trend analysis add detail about which standards students have mastered and how groups of students change over years.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, teachers use standards mastery dashboards to see which standards each student has mastered and to plan small groups and reteaching. The dashboards are only as good as the assessments behind them, so a standard measured by a single question gives a weak picture of mastery. Cohort trend analysis follows groups of students over years, and a district might ask whether students who entered kindergarten in a certain year are doing better in third grade than earlier groups. AI can help analyze these trends in district data platforms. The results guide long term planning and show whether changes are working. The text does not give separate grade band examples.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or finding for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. It states plainly that growth data shows how much students have learned over time and proficiency data shows where they stand against a standard, and that both matter. It also states that a school whose students start far behind may show strong growth even while proficiency remains low. The guidance that reports should show both, so progress is not hidden and gaps are not ignored, is presented as practice rather than as a research result.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits on how much these tools can be trusted. Standards mastery dashboards are only as good as the assessments behind them, and a standard measured by a single question gives a weak picture of mastery. Reports must show both growth and proficiency, so progress is not hidden and gaps are not ignored. Cohort trend analysis results guide long term planning and show whether changes are working, but the text does not say the analysis makes decisions on its own. The decisions about what to report, how to reteach and how to plan remain with the people using the data.
